strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of GUI agents: text-only world models omit spatial and visual information needed for planning. Predicting future GUI images is a relevant and potentially useful direction.

The Symbolic Text Representation is an intuitive decomposition of GUI generation into layout/graphics prediction and language-based text prediction. It directly targets the well-known difficulty diffusion models have rendering small text.

The experiments cover several perspectives—visual similarity, instruction following, trajectory synthesis, and downstream action selection—and include multiple language- and vision-based baselines. The qualitative examples generally show visually coherent state transitions.
The manuscript is easy to follow, and the appendix provides prompts, dataset statistics, additional agent results, and illustrative successes and failures.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is not sufficiently reliable. Two of the three GUI-quality components rely on an unspecified LLM judge without human validation or agreement analysis. More seriously, the action-readiness prompt lists the permitted answer as "yes" or "yes," which can strongly bias or invalidate that metric. The trajectory protocol also inconsistently states that a "yes" under a success/failure field is counted as a match.

The evaluation is small and statistically underdeveloped: the main analysis samples only 57 episodes, reports no confidence intervals or significance tests, and shows downstream gains of only a few absolute percentage points. Repeating one sampled evaluation three times addresses LLM randomness but not sampling uncertainty.

Train, validation, and test splits all contain the same 19 applications and appear to be formed by splitting episodes. Consequently, near-duplicate screens, application templates, and transitions may cross splits. The claimed generalization is supported only by cherry-picked qualitative examples—some of which appear semantically implausible—rather than held-out applications, tasks, or interaction patterns.

The downstream comparison is confounded by extra inference and search. ViMo-enhanced agents generate multiple candidate actions, simulate each one, and invoke an additional LLM-based two-stage selector, while the no-world-model agents apparently do not receive an equivalent candidate-ranking budget. This does not isolate whether improvements arise from the visual world model, additional LLM calls, or search.

Baseline construction and implementation details are inadequate for assessing fairness or reproducibility. The paper does not clearly specify the LLM and diffusion checkpoints, training hyperparameters, image resolution, number of candidate actions, inference cost, baseline adaptation/training procedures, judge model, or prompts/configurations used consistently across comparisons. The advertised project link is blank.

The ablation study does not isolate the proposed components cleanly: its outcome is downstream agent accuracy rather than direct STR/layout/text quality, and the row without either component equals the no-world-model agent performance, leaving unclear whether it represents a functioning ablated world model. There are no OCR, text-symbol detection, text-generation, or oracle-layout ablations to locate errors across the pipeline.

The novelty is useful but incremental: the main construction combines an InstructPix2Pix-style conditional diffusion model, OCR-derived placeholders, and an LLM for text filling and action selection. Given the limited and flawed evaluation, the paper does not yet establish that this composition constitutes a robust visual world model competitive at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: predicting visual GUI transitions could support planning for mobile agents while avoiding the cost and risks of real-device execution.
Separating layout/graphics generation from text generation through the Symbolic Text Representation is intuitive and practically motivated by diffusion models' poor rendering of small text.
The manuscript evaluates several aspects of the system, including visual similarity, instruction following, trajectory synthesis, agent-action accuracy, ablations, and qualitative failure cases.
The reported results are consistently positive: ViMo attains the best aggregate GUI-quality score and improves the reported step accuracy of T3A and M3A.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not convincingly establish the central claim that ViMo improves long-horizon planning. The main downstream metric is offline per-step action accuracy, not end-to-end task success in an interactive environment. The trajectory experiment is also based on LLM judgments against recorded actions and contains only 57 sampled episodes; accuracy rapidly falls to 12.28% at four steps.

There is a serious risk of target leakage in the world-model evaluation. Appendix G.6 states that AITW action instructions are generated using both the current and ground-truth next screenshots. These instructions condition ViMo and may reveal information about the target transition that would not be available in a genuine deployment.

The agent comparison does not isolate the benefit of visual prediction. ViMo introduces candidate generation and a multi-stage LLM reranker, but the paper lacks a matched baseline that applies the same reranking procedure using the current screenshot and action descriptions without generated future GUIs. Gains could therefore arise from additional LLM inference or candidate reranking rather than from the learned world model.

The GUI metrics are insufficiently validated. DINO similarity is insensitive to exact text and functional state, while instructional accuracy, action readiness, trajectory correctness, and action selection rely heavily on unspecified LLM judges. No human-agreement study, judge sensitivity analysis, exact text accuracy, element localization metric, or executable-state validation is provided.

The test scope is narrow and potentially non-independent: all splits cover the same 19 apps, the split construction is not sufficiently detailed to rule out closely related trajectories or repeated states, and there is no held-out-app evaluation. The anecdotal cross-app examples do not establish generalization and sometimes synthesize implausible interfaces rather than faithful environment dynamics.

Comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. Several baselines were adapted from substantially different settings, training and adaptation details are sparse, and there is no evidence that each baseline received comparable data or tuning. TextDiffuser-2 appears qualitatively but is omitted from quantitative comparisons.

The ablations do not directly measure the proposed components' effects on layout, text, or transition accuracy. In particular, the configuration with both components removed is simply reported at the original agents' accuracy, making it unclear whether all rows represent comparable ViMo variants.

Reproducibility is poor: the project link is blank; the precise diffusion checkpoint, LLM identities and versions, decoding settings, training hyperparameters, candidate count, costs, and code/data release are absent. Some appendix prompts contain malformed or contradictory output specifications, further undermining confidence in the LLM-based evaluation.

The claimed practical significance is overstated given the small absolute downstream gains, absence of uncertainty or significance tests, low multi-step accuracy, documented symbol-detection failures, and lack of real-environment task-success results. Overall, the idea is promising, but the current evidence is not competitive for acceptance at a top-tier conference.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of GUI agents: existing world models generally provide textual predictions that omit spatial and visual details needed for planning.

The Symbolic Text Representation is a sensible and useful design. Separating graphical transition prediction from text generation directly targets a well-motivated failure mode of pixel-based GUI generators.

The evaluation is broader than a single image-quality benchmark: it considers visual consistency, instruction compliance, action readiness, trajectory synthesis, and downstream action selection across several agents.

ViMo consistently improves the reported aggregate results over language-based and visual baselines, including gains for both T3A and M3A. The qualitative examples also demonstrate plausible interface transitions and substantially cleaner text than diffusion-only baselines.
The appendix includes prompts, dataset statistics, full-test-set GUI-quality results, repeated-run results, additional agents, qualitative samples, and acknowledged failure cases.
weaknesses: The downstream evidence is not yet sufficient to establish improved real-world, long-horizon agent performance. Evaluation uses offline step accuracy and LLM-judged agreement with reference actions rather than end-to-end task success in an interactive emulator. Errors from recursively predicted states and recovery behavior are therefore not tested.

The principal semantic metrics rely on an unspecified LLM judge without human-agreement measurements, judge sensitivity analysis, or evaluation against objective environment states. The action-readiness prompt is also malformed: it asks for the value to be either "yes" or "yes", undermining confidence in this metric.

The dataset split contains the same 19 apps in training, validation, and testing. Consequently, the experiments mainly measure generalization to held-out episodes within known apps, while claims about novel combinations and real-world applicability are based largely on qualitative examples. Evaluation on unseen apps, layouts, or app versions is needed.

Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript does not clearly identify the LLMs used for text prediction, action generation, selection, and judging, and omits important diffusion training and inference hyperparameters, computational costs, latency, and API settings. The displayed project link is blank.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled. Adding ViMo introduces extra LLM calls and a separate selection procedure, but there is no compute-matched baseline using outcome reasoning or self-critique without generated images. HTML rendering is also a weak proxy for stronger structured or multimodal GUI-transition models.

The evaluation samples are modest for agent conclusions, uncertainty or significance intervals are absent, and the headline relative gains can overstate fairly small absolute improvements—for example, 46.01 to 50.16 for M3A.

The ablation study reports only downstream action accuracy and does not isolate OCR errors, STR localization quality, GUI-text prediction accuracy, or the contributions of individual LLM stages. Figure 11 shows that malformed symbols can cause conspicuous failures, but their frequency and downstream impact are not quantified.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: predicting visual GUI transitions could provide richer planning signals than textual world models for mobile agents.

The separation of layout/graphics prediction from exact text generation through Symbolic Text Representation is intuitive and practically motivated. Qualitative examples suggest it reduces the visibly corrupted text produced by pixel-only baselines.

The evaluation is broad in scope, covering GUI quality, several app-agent backbones, alternative world models, unseen apps, online AndroidWorld tasks, multi-step rollouts, human judgments, ablations, runtime, and failure cases.
The appendix provides useful prompts, dataset counts, full-test results for the generation metrics, and some implementation details.
weaknesses: The central agent-improvement evidence is substantially confounded. ViMo augmentation introduces candidate-action generation followed by multiple additional LLM evaluation and selection calls, but the no-world-model agents do not receive a compute- or query-matched deliberation baseline. Much of the reported gain could therefore come from extra inference-time reasoning rather than visual prediction. Indeed, alternative world models recover most of the improvement, while ViMo's advantage over the strongest such baselines is only about 1 percentage point in several tables and is unsupported by significance tests.

The evaluation scale and statistical treatment are inadequate for the claimed superiority. The main decision experiment uses only 57 sampled episodes, the human study uses just 20 generated examples per method, and no confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, inter-rater agreement, or per-task paired analysis are reported. Small differences in Tables 2, 3, and 9 may readily reflect sampling or LLM variability.

The standard train, validation, and test splits contain the same 19 apps, making the main results vulnerable to memorization of highly repetitive app layouts. The purported zero-shot evaluation does not specify the held-out apps, sample counts, overlap checks, or uncertainty, so it does not convincingly establish generalization.

Generation quality is measured mainly by DINO similarity and GPT-based binary judgments. DINO similarity does not directly test whether interactive elements, text, or transition semantics are correct, while the LLM judge may share biases with the GPT-based text predictor and action-selection pipeline. The human-study assignment, randomization, blinding, and aggregation procedures are also insufficiently described.

The long-horizon motivation is only weakly addressed: the deployed method predicts one step by default, and recursive rollout performance rapidly collapses. The paper does not model stochastic or multimodal transition outcomes, maintain latent state beyond the screenshot, or evaluate calibrated transition likelihoods.

The technical novelty is limited to a useful but fairly simple placeholder representation combined with an existing image-conditioned diffusion model, OCR, handcrafted rendering, and a proprietary multimodal LLM. There is little new learning methodology or formal treatment of GUI dynamics.

Reproducibility is poor for a model-training paper: the project link is blank, release is only promised, and essential details such as the exact diffusion checkpoint, image resolution, optimizer, learning rate, schedule, epochs, sampling settings, data filtering rules, and costs are absent. Heavy dependence on changing proprietary GPT/Gemini models compounds the problem.

Claims such as 'real-time,' 'lightweight,' and a new benchmark are overstated given roughly two additional minutes per three-action request, incomplete dataset-release information, and the absence of a standardized benchmark protocol. The proposed access commitment is also only a vague safeguard against misuse.

strengths: The core idea is intuitive and potentially useful: separating GUI graphics/layout generation from text reconstruction directly addresses a genuine weakness of pixel-space image generators.

The evaluation considers several relevant dimensions, including visual quality, action consistency, downstream decision accuracy, zero-shot applications, online navigation, runtime, and comparisons across multiple agents and world-model baselines.
The reported online improvement from 33.19% to 40.95% task success is promising, and several qualitative examples are visually plausible.
weaknesses: The AITW preprocessing creates action instructions using both the current and ground-truth next screenshots. Applying this procedure to test examples gives the conditioning instruction privileged information about the prediction target, compromising the validity of the central GUI-generation evaluation.

The empirical evidence lacks statistical support. The primary evaluation uses only 57 sampled episodes, sample counts for several downstream tables are unclear, and no confidence intervals, significance tests, or task-level variance are reported. Consequently, small advantages such as 50.16% versus 48.89% step accuracy are not demonstrably meaningful.

Evaluation is substantially circular: GPT-4o contributes to action-instruction creation, GUI text generation, action selection, and the instructional-accuracy/action-readiness judgments. There is no validation of the LLM judge against independent annotations, while DINO similarity is poorly suited to measuring exact GUI text and functional correctness.

The user study evaluates only 20 generated samples per method and omits important protocol details such as sample assignment, participant expertise, inter-rater agreement, uncertainty estimates, compensation, and ethics approval. These omissions make the very large claimed relative human-evaluation gains difficult to interpret.

The long-horizon motivation is not convincingly supported. The main method selects actions from one-step predictions, the authors ultimately use one rollout step, and full-trajectory accuracy deteriorates to 12.28% by four steps. This is evidence of severe compounding error rather than reliable long-horizon planning.

The ablations do not isolate the principal claimed contributions. There is no controlled comparison of STR against alternative structured/layout representations, no removal or replacement of the GUI-text predictor, and no systematic analysis of OCR, symbol-detection, or text-rendering errors. Baseline adaptation and tuning parity are also insufficiently documented.

Generalization claims are underspecified: the main train/validation/test splits contain the same 19 applications, while the zero-shot evaluation does not report the held-out applications, task counts, overlap controls, or uncertainty. A few deliberately unusual qualitative prompts are not compelling evidence of robust generalization.

Reproducibility is weak. The project link is blank, release is only promised, and essential training details such as the precise diffusion checkpoint, resolution, optimization schedule, compute budget, decoding settings, and exact proprietary-model versions are missing.

Calling the system lightweight and suitable for real-time interaction is questionable: evaluating three candidate actions takes roughly two minutes in addition to agent latency and depends on remote proprietary LLM calls.

The social-impact discussion does not address the privacy implications of sending potentially sensitive screenshots and OCR-derived text to cloud LLMs. Requiring a user commitment before checkpoint access is not a substantive misuse safeguard.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: visual prediction of future mobile-GUI states for agent planning. Separating layout/graphics prediction from text generation through the Symbolic Text Representation is simple, well motivated, and practically useful.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering visual quality, human judgments, downstream action selection, unseen applications, online AndroidWorld navigation, multi-step rollouts, runtime, ablations, and qualitative failure cases.

The downstream results consistently favor ViMo across several agents and world-model baselines. Particularly encouraging are the T3A step-accuracy improvement from 43.13% to 49.20% and the AndroidWorld task-success improvement from 33.19% to 40.95%.
The paper is clear and well organized. The architecture, inference procedure, prompts, dataset composition, full-test evaluation, and randomness study are documented in substantial detail.
The authors acknowledge error accumulation and malformed text-symbol failures rather than presenting only successful examples.
weaknesses: The agent gains are not cleanly attributable to the visual world model. ViMo adds a multi-stage LLM selector with repeated scoring and comparison calls, but there is no decisive ablation using the same selector without informative predicted GUIs, with the current GUI, or with ground-truth future GUIs.

Much of the evidence relies on GPT-4o-based generation or judging. The custom instructional-accuracy and action-readiness metrics are only weakly validated, and using closely related LLMs throughout the pipeline risks correlated bias. Standard text-fidelity measures such as OCR accuracy or edit distance are also absent.

The human study lacks important methodological information: samples appear to be different across methods rather than matched by input, and the paper does not report randomization, blinding, per-sample annotation counts, inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

Several headline differences are modest and reported without uncertainty. This is especially consequential for the 57-episode sampled evaluation, the world-model comparison around 48–50% step accuracy, and the single online comparison on 116 tasks.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: essential diffusion training details such as the precise backbone/version, image resolution, optimization schedule, epochs, sampling configuration, and compute budget are missing, while code and checkpoints are only promised for a future release.

The claim of practical or real-time deployment is overstated: evaluating three candidate actions takes roughly two additional minutes per decision. The zero-shot and long-horizon results are promising, but they remain limited in scale and degrade sharply with rollout length.
